description: This chapter explains why the French Revolution happened, what happened during it, and how it changed France and the world. It matters because it shows how ordinary people can overthrow unfair systems — a pattern that repeats in history.

sections.title: French Society During the Late Eighteenth Century
sections.summary: Introduces the three-estate system, the financial crisis under Louis XVI, and the social inequalities that set the stage for revolution.
diagrams: Figure 3 — The Spider and the Fly

subsections.title: The Struggle to Survive
subsections.summary: Population growth, rising bread prices, and the widening gap between rich and poor leading to subsistence crises.

subsections.title: How a Subsistence Crisis Happens
subsections.summary: The chain reaction from bad harvest to food riots, illustrated as a flow diagram.
diagrams: Figure 4 — The course of a subsistence crisis

subsections.title: A Growing Middle Class Envisages an End to Privileges
subsections.summary: The emergence of the educated middle class and Enlightenment ideas from Locke, Rousseau, and Montesquieu that challenged feudal privilege.

sections.title: The Outbreak of the Revolution
sections.summary: The calling of the Estates General, the Third Estate's walkout, the Tennis Court Oath, the storming of the Bastille, and the Great Fear in the countryside.
diagrams: Figure 6 — The spread of the Great Fear

subsections.title: France Becomes a Constitutional Monarchy
subsections.summary: The Constitution of 1791, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen, and the new political system separating powers.
keyTerms: Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen
diagrams: Figure 7 — The Political system under the Constitution of 1791
Figure 8 — The Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen

sections.title: France Abolishes Monarchy and Becomes a Republic
sections.summary: The war against Prussia and Austria, the rise of the Jacobins, the storming of the Tuileries, the execution of the king, and France becoming a republic.

subsections.title: The Reign of Terror
subsections.summary: Robespierre's policy of severe control and punishment, the guillotine, wage/price controls, and his eventual downfall.

subsections.title: A Directory Rules France
subsections.summary: The fall of the Jacobins, the new constitution, the Directory system, and the political instability that led to Napoleon's rise.

sections.title: Did Women have a Revolution?
sections.summary: Women's participation in the revolution, their demands for equal rights, Olympe de Gouges, and the eventual closure of women's clubs.
keyTerms: Society of Revolutionary and Republican Women
Declaration of the Rights of Woman and Citizen
diagrams: Figure 12 — Parisian women on their way to Versailles
Figure 13 — Women queuing up at a bakery

sections.title: The Abolition of Slavery
sections.summary: The triangular slave trade, the Convention's 1794 legislation to free slaves, Napoleon's reintroduction of slavery, and final abolition in 1848.

sections.title: The Revolution and Everyday Life
sections.summary: The abolition of censorship, freedom of the press, and how revolutionary ideas spread through print, plays, and festivals.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Napoleon's rise and fall, the legacy of liberty and democratic rights spreading across Europe, and the impact on Indian reformers like Raja Rammohan Roy.
